unit-ww503.title: Wordly Wise · Lesson 3
unit-ww503.source: Wordly Wise 3000 Book 5, Lesson 3 (PDF in Drive)

summary.text: The fifteen words of Lesson 3: ancestor, carnivore, comprehend, duration, evident, extinct, ferocious, gigantic, obscure, option, premature, preserve, prey, puny, and survive — plus the related forms the book teaches (carnivorous, comprehension, ferocity, optional, survivor). A very animal-flavored list: predators, prey, and things that went extinct.

why.text: This lesson's words show up constantly in science reading — extinct, carnivore, prey, survive, preserve are exactly the vocabulary of nature units. New this lesson: some questions ask you to TYPE the word, because knowing a word and spelling it are two different muscles and quizzes test both.

objectives.text: Give the meaning of all fifteen Lesson 3 words in fresh sentences.
Tell the multiple meanings apart: extinct species vs. extinct volcano, obscure hidden vs. obscure hard-to-understand, prey the animal vs. prey the verb.
Use the related forms — carnivorous, comprehension, ferocity, optional, survivor — as comfortably as the base words.
Spell the hardest five correctly from memory.

parentNote.text: Built from the Lesson 3 scan in Drive. Definitions match the workbook; quiz sentences are fresh, so the workbook exercises stay her homework. This is the first unit with type-the-word spelling questions (five of them, on the hardest spellings: ferocious, gigantic, comprehend, obscure, premature) — they're excluded from Beat-the-clock automatically, and a misspelling goes to the Growth Zone like any other miss. The multi-meaning words to listen for at dinner: extinct (species AND volcanoes), obscure (hidden AND confusing), prey (noun AND verb).

nextUp.text: Cards once, then a quiz round a day. The spelling questions want a real keyboard moment — no autocorrect rescue on the real quiz.

cards.def:
**A person from whom one is descended.** (noun)
• Second meaning: an early kind of animal from which later ones developed — a forerunner.
• The dog-sized mesohippus is an ancestor of the modern horse.
cards.hint: Your family tree going UP — and a species' family tree going back.

cards.def:
**A flesh-eating animal.** (noun)
• carnivorous (adj.): flesh-eating — 'dogs are carnivorous but eat other foods too.'
• Sharp, pointed teeth are the giveaway.
cards.hint: Carne means meat — a carnivore is a meat-eater.

cards.def:
**To understand.** (verb)
• comprehension (noun): the act or ability of understanding.
• You can comprehend a language better than you speak it.
cards.hint: Reading comprehension = did you UNDERSTAND what you read.

cards.def:
**The time during which something lasts or continues.** (noun)
• 'For the duration of the storm' = the whole time it lasted.
cards.hint: How long it endures — duration and endure share a root.

cards.def:
**Easy to see and understand; obvious, clear.** (adjective)
• 'It is evident from your face that you're happy.' The evidence is right there.
cards.hint: Evident and evidence: what the proof makes plain.

cards.def:
**No longer existing or living.** (adjective)
• Second meaning: no longer active — Mount St. Helens was called an extinct volcano until 1980 proved otherwise.
• Species and volcanoes share this word.
cards.hint: Extinguished — the flame is out, for mammoths and mountains alike.

cards.def:
**Savage; fierce.** (adjective)
• ferocity (noun): the state or quality of being fierce — 'the ferocity of the storm.'
• Guard dogs and storms both qualify.
cards.hint: Fero- like feral — wild with teeth.

cards.def:
**Very large; like a giant in size.** (adjective)
• The Spruce Goose was a gigantic airplane that made exactly one flight.

**To cover up or keep from being seen.** (verb)
• As an adjective: hard to see ('an obscure shape in the mist') — or hard to understand ('obscure words like cauldron and phoenix').
• One word, three jobs.
cards.hint: Clouds obscure the moon; strange words obscure the meaning.

cards.def:
**A choice, or something available as a choice.** (noun)
• optional (adj.): left to choice — 'lunch was required, dinner was optional.'
cards.hint: Opt = choose. Options are the things you may opt for.

cards.def:
**Too early; happening or arriving before the proper time.** (adjective)
• Premature babies arrive early; a premature celebration happens before the win is real.

**To save; to keep from harm; to protect.** (verb)
• Second meaning: to keep from rotting or spoiling — preserving peaches by canning.
• Laws preserve forests; jars preserve fruit.
cards.hint: Pre-SERVE: keep it safe so it can serve later.

cards.def:
**An animal that is hunted for food.** (noun)
• Also: a victim — 'prey to thieves.'
• As a verb: to hunt for food, or to rob using violence or trickery — 'wolves prey on the weakest deer.'
cards.hint: Prey is the hunted; the predator does the preying. (Don't spell it 'pray.')

cards.def:
**Weak.** (adjective)
• Second meaning: lacking in size, strength, or power — 'my one-dollar offering seemed puny.'
cards.hint: The opposite of gigantic, two cards up.

cards.def:
**To stay alive where there is a chance of dying.** (verb)
• Also: to continue existing through a threatening situation — two of eight maples survived the hurricane.
• survivor (noun): one who stays alive where others do not.
cards.hint: Sur- (through) + vive (live): to live through it.

questions.q: The woolly mammoth has been ___ for about ten thousand years.
questions.hint: There are no woolly mammoths anywhere. Which word says that?
steps: Find the clue: mammoths no longer exist at all.
Match: extinct means no longer existing or living.
Check the impostors: ferocious is fierce, premature is too early, obscure is hidden — none mean gone forever.

ex.main: **Extinct.** Gone as a species — the word for 'none left, anywhere, ever.'
ex.tip: Extinct is permanent and total. One surviving pair means a species is endangered, not extinct.

questions.q: Scientists call the dog-sized mesohippus an ___ of the modern horse. Which meaning of the word is that?
opts: ancestor — the animal-forerunner meaning, not the family-tree-of-people meaning
ancestor — a person you are descended from
questions.hint: Nobody is related to a mesohippus — but a species can be.
steps: Ancestor has two meanings: a person in your family line, and an early animal form that later ones developed from.
A mesohippus is an animal, not a person — so it is the forerunner meaning.
The book's own example is exactly this horse.

ex.main: **Ancestor, the forerunner sense.** Species have family trees too — the second meaning covers evolution, not genealogy.
ex.tip: When a person-word gets used for animals or things, check the entry for a second meaning. Wordly Wise loves testing those.

questions.q: Sharp, pointed teeth for tearing meat tell you an animal is a ___.
questions.hint: Meat-eater.
steps: The clue is the toolkit: tearing teeth exist for eating flesh.
A flesh-eating animal is a carnivore.
Prey is the hunted, not the hunter — the tempting wrong answer flips the roles.

ex.main: **Carnivore.** The teeth are the tell — the book's own example.
ex.tip: Carnivore/prey questions are role questions: who is eating whom?

questions.q: Which sentence uses 'carnivorous' correctly?
opts: The carnivorous placed meat in the cage.
A salad is a carnivorous meal.
Bears eat berries too, so they are carnivorous only part of the time.
Though bears eat berries and fish alike, their sharp teeth mark them as carnivorous.
questions.hint: Carnivorous is an ADJECTIVE — it has to describe something.
steps: Carnivorous is the adjective form: it must describe a noun (a carnivorous animal, a carnivorous diet).
'The carnivorous placed meat in the cage' uses it as a noun; the salad sentence calls a salad flesh-eating — backwards.
'Carnivorous only part of the time' misuses the meaning — it is about diet type, not a schedule.
The sharp-teeth sentence describes bears with it correctly — the book itself notes carnivorous animals often eat other foods too.

ex.main: **The bears sentence.** Adjective doing adjective work, and the meaning survives — the book's dog example makes the same point.
ex.tip: For related-form questions, check the JOB first (noun? adjective?), then the meaning.

questions.q: We stayed inside for the ___ of the thunderstorm — all forty-five minutes of it.
questions.hint: The whole time it lasted.
steps: The clue: the entire time the storm went on.
Duration is the time during which something lasts.
Ferocity is tempting because storms are fierce — but the sentence measures TIME, not fierceness.

ex.main: **Duration.** 'For the duration of' is practically a set phrase — the whole stretch of time.
ex.tip: When a sentence counts minutes, pick the time word even if a drama word is on offer.

questions.q: Nobody had to announce the winner — from the cheering, it was ___ who won.
questions.hint: So clear that no announcement was needed.
steps: The clue: the answer was obvious without being said.
Evident means easy to see and understand; obvious.
Obscure is its exact opposite — a nice trap sitting right there.

ex.main: **Evident.** Evident and obscure are opposites; this list carries both on purpose.
ex.tip: Learn opposing pairs together — evident/obscure, gigantic/puny. Half the quiz is telling them apart.

questions.q: 'The instructions were so obscure that even Dad read them three times.' Which meaning of 'obscure' is that?
opts: To cover up or keep from being seen
Hard to see; hidden in shadow
questions.hint: The instructions are visible — the problem is elsewhere.
steps: Obscure has three jobs: verb (to hide), adjective (hard to SEE), adjective (hard to UNDERSTAND).
Nothing is hidden from view here — the words are being read, three times.
The struggle is comprehension, so it is the not-easy-to-understand sense — the book's example is a story full of words like 'cauldron' and 'phoenix.'

ex.main: **Not easy to understand.** Same test as always for multi-meaning words: what is actually failing — the eyes or the understanding?
ex.tip: Obscure instructions, obscure words, obscure explanation → the understanding sense. Obscure shape, obscure figure → the seeing sense.

questions.q: The new cruise ship was ___ — longer than three football fields.
questions.hint: Giant-sized.
steps: The clue: enormous size, spelled out in football fields.
Gigantic means very large; like a giant.
The others don't describe size at all.

ex.main: **Gigantic.** Size, pure and simple — 'giant' is visible inside the word.
ex.tip: When the sentence measures something huge, look for the word with 'giant' in it.

questions.q: Which word fits BOTH blanks: 'The ___ of the guard dog surprised us' and 'The storm hit with unexpected ___'?
questions.hint: Fierceness — of an animal AND of weather.
steps: First blank: a guard dog's fierceness — ferocity, the noun form of ferocious.
Second blank: the book's own example is 'the ferocity of the storm.'
Test the others in both blanks: a storm's comprehension? A dog's option? Only ferocity survives both.

ex.main: **Ferocity.** The noun form of ferocious stretches from animals to storms — fierceness wherever it lives.
ex.tip: Both-blanks questions test the word's core idea. Find what the two sentences share (fierceness) and match it.

questions.q: 'Coming to practice is required, but the team dinner is ___.' The missing word is:
questions.hint: Left to choice.
steps: The sentence contrasts required with its opposite.
Optional means left to choice — the adjective form of option.
The book's example has the same shape: lunch required, dinner optional.

ex.main: **Optional.** Required vs. optional is the contrast the sentence is built on.
ex.tip: Contrast sentences ('but...') hand you the answer: find the word that opposes the first half.

questions.q: Celebrating at halftime turned out to be ___ — the other team scored three times after the break.
questions.hint: The celebration came before it was safe to celebrate.
steps: The clue: they celebrated too early, before the outcome was settled.
Premature means happening before the proper time.
Pre- (before) + mature (ready): the celebration wasn't ready to happen.

ex.main: **Premature.** Not wrong to celebrate — wrong to celebrate THEN. The word is entirely about timing.
ex.tip: Premature marks timing errors: premature celebration, premature conclusion, premature baby — early every time.

questions.q: 'Grandma preserves the summer tomatoes in glass jars.' Which meaning of 'preserve' is that?
opts: To keep from rotting or spoiling
questions.hint: What do the jars actually prevent?
steps: Preserve has two senses: protect from harm (preserve the forests) and keep from spoiling (preserve the peaches).
Jars and canning fight rot, not robbers.
The keep-from-spoiling sense — the book's example is canned peaches, same move.

ex.main: **Keep from spoiling.** Both senses are about saving something — the question is saving it from WHAT. Jars answer: from rot.
ex.tip: Preserve + food = the spoiling sense. Preserve + forests/traditions/buildings = the protect sense.

questions.q: In which sentence is 'prey' used as a VERB?
opts: The rabbit is easy prey for the hawk.
Scammers prey on people who are in a hurry.
The lion watched its prey from the tall grass.
Travelers can be prey to pickpockets.
questions.hint: The verb is the ACT of hunting or robbing — something the subject DOES.
steps: Prey the noun names the hunted; prey the verb is the hunting (or robbing) itself.
'Easy prey', 'its prey', 'prey to pickpockets' — all name a thing or victim. Nouns.
'Scammers prey on people' — preying is what the scammers DO. That's the verb, in the book's rob-by-trickery sense.

ex.main: **'Scammers prey on people.'** The verb form usually travels with 'on' — to prey ON someone. And note the spelling: prey, never pray.
ex.tip: The 'prey on' construction is the verb's fingerprint. No 'on', probably the noun.

questions.q: Next to the weightlifter's barbell, my backpack looked ___.
questions.hint: Small and weak by comparison.
steps: The clue: something looks small and weak next to something mighty.
Puny means weak, or lacking in size or power.
The book's example is the same shape: a one-dollar offering seeming puny next to bigger gifts.

ex.main: **Puny.** Puny is comparative by nature — things look puny NEXT TO something bigger.
ex.tip: Puny and gigantic are this lesson's size bookends. Expect them played against each other.

questions.q: Which sentence uses 'survivor' correctly?
opts: The survivor of the storm rebuilt fastest of all.
It was a survivor day for everyone.
questions.hint: Survivor is a NOUN — a person or thing that lived through it.
steps: Survivor is the noun form: one who stays alive or comes through a situation.
'She survivor the long winter' and 'The plants survivor without water' need the verb survive; 'a survivor day' wrongly uses it as an adjective.
Only 'The survivor of the storm' treats it as a noun naming a person — correct.

ex.main: **'The survivor of the storm…'** Verb: survive. Noun: survivor. The -or ending names the one who did it, like sailor and inventor.
ex.tip: -or/-er endings usually mean 'the one who does it.' If the sentence needs an action, you want the bare verb instead.

questions.q: Spell the word that means savage; fierce.
questions.hint: It ends the same way as 'delicious.'
steps: Break it into syllables: fe · ro · cious.
The tricky part is the ending: -cious, like delicious and precious.
ferocious.

ex.main: **ferocious.** The -cious ending is the trap — not -tious, not -teous.
ex.tip: Rhyme it with delicious in your head; they end identically.

questions.q: Spell the word that means very large; like a giant.
questions.hint: Giant is inside it — but the first G and the second G sound different.
steps: Start from the word hiding inside: giant → gigantic.
Two g's: the first says J, the second says G — gi · gan · tic.
gigantic.

ex.main: **gigantic.** One word, two different g-sounds — spell it by the built-in 'giant.'
ex.tip: If you can spell giant, add gi- in front and -ic behind.

questions.q: Spell the word that means to understand.
questions.hint: Three syllables you already say in 'reading ___-sion.'
steps: Syllables: com · pre · hend.
No double letters anywhere — the temptation is an extra m or a sneaky 'a.'
comprehend.

ex.main: **comprehend.** Clean syllable-by-syllable spelling — com, pre, hend, no doubles.
ex.tip: Spell long words one syllable at a time; almost every letter earns its place.

questions.q: Spell the word that means hard to see, or hard to understand.
questions.hint: The middle has a hidden 's-c' pair.
steps: Syllables: ob · scure.
The trap is the sc together — obSCure, like 'score' with an s in front.
obscure.

ex.main: **obscure.** The sc pair is the whole test — ob + scure.
ex.tip: Think 'ob + secure minus the e': the shape is nearly the same.

questions.q: Spell the word that means too early; before the proper time.
questions.hint: Two pieces you already know: pre + mature.
steps: It is built from parts: pre- (before) + mature (ready).
Both parts are spelled exactly as you know them — no letters change at the seam.
premature.

ex.main: **premature.** Prefix words spell themselves if you know the pieces: pre + mature.
ex.tip: When a word is prefix + word-you-know, spell the pieces, not the whole.
